tagline: Social posts get approved by the client before anything goes near a publish button.
verdictSummary: Planable is not really a scheduler, it is an approval workflow that happens to publish at the end. The approval half is buildable in a weekend: a shareable read-only link, comments per post, an approve button, and a rule that nothing enters the queue until it is signed off. The publish half is where the days go, because that is one platform app review per network, and the pixel-accurate previews clients actually approve against need rebuilding every time a network changes its layout.
coreLoopDIY: Draft posts into a campaign, send a reviewer a link that needs no account, collect their approvals and comments, and let only approved posts enter the publishing queue.
whatYouLose: previews that match each network pixel for pixel
every network beyond the one you got API approval for
multi-stage approval chains and per-workspace roles
the shared media library across clients
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the approval trail is the deliverable. When a client says they never signed off on that post, the timestamped record is what ends the conversation, and an agency will pay for that alone.
notes: Approval-first framing, deliberately different from the other social schedulers in this catalogue: publishing is the last step here, not the product.
prompt:
Build a social content approval tool where publishing is the final step, not the main feature.

Content model: a campaign holds posts. A post has text, attached media, a target network, an intended publish time and a status: draft, in review, changes requested, approved, scheduled, published, failed.

Review flow, which is the core of this build. Generating a review link creates a signed, expiring URL that opens a read-only board with no account required. The reviewer sees each post rendered in an approximation of its target network's layout, and can approve it or request changes with a comment. Every action writes an immutable event: who (by the name they typed on first visit), what, when, and against which version of the post text. Editing an approved post resets it to draft and records why — this rule is the whole point, and it must not be bypassable from the admin side either.

Collaboration: internal comments visible only to the operator, separate from reviewer comments. A diff view showing what changed between the version the reviewer approved and the current text.

Publishing: connect exactly one network through its documented OAuth flow. Only posts in the approved state can be scheduled. A background worker publishes at the scheduled time with an idempotency key, stores the returned post ID, and moves the post to published or failed with the error text preserved. A failed post is never retried silently.

Export: a per-campaign PDF or HTML report containing every post, its final text, and its full approval trail with timestamps. This is what gets attached to an invoice.

Out of scope: connecting a second network, scraping or unofficial APIs, analytics on published posts, a shared asset library, and multi-stage approval chains. One reviewer, one approval, one record.

faq.q: Can I import my Planable content?
faq.a: Planable exports posts as CSV, so text and scheduled times come across. Approval history does not export, which matters because that history is the reason to use the tool at all — old campaigns stay in Planable if you need to be able to prove anything about them.

faq.q: How close can the previews get?
faq.a: Close enough to catch a truncated caption or a badly cropped image, which is most of what review is for. They will not be pixel-accurate, and they will drift as networks redesign. If a client approves on appearance rather than content, this is where the build shows its seams.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: A small VPS with PostgreSQL, five to ten dollars a month, plus media storage. Review links cost nothing and reviewers do not need accounts, so the number of clients does not change the bill.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Working across networks. An agency posts to five platforms for one client, and this build handles one. Adding the second is a separate developer account and a separate app review, which is weeks of waiting rather than an afternoon of coding.
